question_type: Variance of six monthly bond-yield values (high-grade corporate, Jan-Jun 1938), with a sample-vs-population ambiguity and one month revised in later printings

opus_divergence.what_opus_did: Opus used the revised series. April 1938 was revised in the July 1941 issue and stayed unchanged through 1947, and the later table's labels 'High-grade corporate bonds' / '(Percent per annum)' match the question's wording. It then took the SAMPLE variance (n-1), treating 'the sample calendar months' as a statistical cue.
opus_divergence.what_right_glm_did: The none arm used the same revised series; it traced the revision to the 1941_07 printing at [42]-[44] and matched the 'percent per annum' label of the later table at [46]. It took the POPULATION variance (n), reading 'sample calendar months' as 'the selected months' and falling back on the default that a bare 'variance' of a listed set is the population variance ([15], [23]).
opus_divergence.evidence: Opus worklog.md:8 (sample variance 'because the question calls the six months the sample'), worklog.md:19-28 (revision found; revised series chosen), solution.json:12-13 (vintage and n-1 decisions), solution.json:16 (population variance listed as an alternative); review.md:5, 20 (reviewer agreed and listed population variance as residual risk (a)); none [13], [15], [23], [44], [46]

reviewer_flag: Verdict 'confirmed'. The reviewer listed the population variance as residual risk (a) and the 1939 vintage as risk (b), and judged both less likely because the question says 'sample' and uses the later table's labels (review.md:20).
right_by_principled_choice_or_luck: Unclear, leaning luck on the formula. At [15] the none arm leaned toward population variance ('variance of listed data = population variance unless specified sample'), but at [23] it wavered (noting that pandas defaults to the sample variance), and at [46] it still listed both candidates before submitting. The vintage half was principled: it followed the row forward to the 1941 revision ([42]-[44]) and chose the printing whose unit label matches the question ([46]).
wrong_glm_arms_same_as_opus: No. Cards and prompt chose the same formula as the right arm, population variance (cards [26], [29]; prompt [11], [17]). They went wrong on vintage, where Opus was right: both took the ORIGINAL 1939 printing with the unrevised April value, so their error is SOURCE_ISSUE_VINTAGE. Cards tried to check the 1941_07 reprint at [30]-[33], read the wrong line range, and dropped the check at [34] ('Need not'). The prompt arm never grepped the row forward, even though its context says to 'grep the row forward, then apply the family's rule'. It then thrashed badly: the same 'Values confirmed ...' THINK appears 32 times between [13] and [77], the run took 726 s, and there was a context-compaction warning at [79]. It submitted after trusting the handoff summary at [80].
lesson_for_harness: This question is on the disputed-answer list, so it should not become a strong rule. It gives only a weak signal that this benchmark's key uses the population variance for a bare 'variance' even when the text says 'sample calendar months', where 'sample' plausibly just means 'selected'. The right mechanism is a formula-ambiguity CHECK that computes both n and n-1 and forces an explicit, logged choice, not a hard-coded convention. The robust lesson is about vintage: Opus and the right arm both traced the row forward to its revision, and both wrong GLM arms failed exactly there. A TOOL that finds all printings of a row, plus a CHECK that the cited printing is the latest carrying it, would have fixed both wrong arms. A CONTROL-level loop detector (the same THINK repeated with no new evidence) would also have cut the prompt arm's 10-minute thrash.
notes: The sample and population variances differ by a factor of 6/5 (about 20%). The unrevised April value makes the variance about a third smaller. So all four combinations of vintage and formula give different answers under exact-match grading, and each arm landed on a different one of them. Because issue47 is true, the official key itself may be questionable, so this reverse case should count only as low-weight evidence against Opus.
